sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva for every Jewish man who wears a garment with four corners to put threads of tzitzit on it, and through the tzitzit being seen on his garments he will remember all the mitzvot and keep away from the desires and errors after which the heart and the eyes are liable to be drawn, and through this Israel will be set apart and sanctified to God. As it is said (Bamidbar 15:37-40): "And the Lord spoke to Moshe, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them that they shall make for themselves tzitzit on the corners of their garments throughout their generations, and they shall put on the tzitzit of the corner a thread of tekhelet. And it shall be for you as tzitzit, and you shall see it and remember all the mitzvot of the Lord and do them, and you shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes, after which you go astray. So that you remember and do all My mitzvot, and be holy to your God." And it is likewise said (Devarim 22:12): "You shall make for yourself twisted threads on the four corners of your covering with which you cover yourself."

Although there is no obligation to buy a garment with four corners and to fulfil the mitzva of tzitzit with it, it is fitting to fulfil this mitzva, which expresses Jewish identity in a way that is visible to all. One can explain that the Torah did not want to oblige the wearing of a garment with tzitzit, so that Israel could of their own accord cherish the mitzva and volunteer to fulfil it, and through this rise up and identify with the faith and grow stronger in keeping all the mitzvot.

The tzitzit are made of white threads, and the Torah commanded to combine in them a thread of tekhelet. In the wake of the exile Israel had difficulty obtaining tekhelet, until in the days of the Geonim the way of preparing it was forgotten, and they fulfilled the mitzva with white threads only. Some hold that today the way to prepare the tekhelet dye has been found, and the mitzva of combining tekhelet in the threads of the tzitzit has returned (below 2:13-17).

The Sages said (Menaḥot 43b): "This mitzva is equal to all the mitzvot together." This is because it reminds one of all the mitzvot, and remembering the mitzvot arouses one to do them, as it is said (Bamidbar 15:39): "and you shall see it and remember all the mitzvot of the Lord and do them." The Sages further said (there): "Whoever is meticulous in this mitzva merits to receive the Divine Presence." For since he sees the tzitzit many times during the day, their memory is engraved on his heart, and even when he is not looking at them, they remind him of all the mitzvot, and one who always remembers them is considered as receiving the Divine Presence (following the Abarbanel, Bamidbar 15).

Since the tzitzit are visible outwardly, every Jew who fulfils the mitzva of tzitzit shows of himself that he cleaves to God and wants to remember and to remind of all His mitzvot, and by this he sanctifies the name of Heaven. This is what is said (Bamidbar 15:40): "and be holy to your God", that through wearing the tzitzit we become sanctified and set apart to God, and recognisable to all as representatives and servants of the King of the universe (Ba'al Ha-Turim there 38; Abarbanel there).1

notes_en.en:
The tasseled tallit, which reminds one of all the mitzvot, surrounds the person, and through this the person merits that the Divine light surrounding the world and the person is clothed in his garment. By means of this 'surrounding light', he can merit to receive protection from the temptations of the inclination and from evil thoughts (following Tzidkat Ha-Tzaddik 220). And see the next halakha.
The Alshikh explained (Bamidbar 15) that there are mitzvot which a person does not have the occasion to fulfil, and their absence causes him to be unable to be sanctified in all his 248 limbs and 365 sinews; and God gave us the mitzva of tzitzit, through which a person remembers all the mitzvot and wants to do them, and this remembrance is considered for him as a deed, and through this he can be sanctified every day in all the mitzvot.

sections.body_en:
The tallit expresses the material world in its four directions, in which mighty forces are hidden. Even in every tiny atom enormous energy is contained. The question is how we can use all these forces without being harmed. Likewise man is a small world, and there are in him enormous desires and talents that can perfect and repair the whole world, and can also turn into inclinations that corrupt man and the world. The question is how we will use all the enormous forces hidden in the world and in man in a way that does good and not harm. The solution is hinted at in the mitzva of tzitzit, whose threads hint at the 613 mitzvot of the Torah (below 2:1), which guide us how to bring into actuality all the forces hidden in man and in the world, in order and in stages, in all areas of life. In other words, the tallit that surrounds a person hints at the 'surrounding light', which is above and beyond our grasp, and it also expresses all the enormous forces hidden within the world (see Peninei Halakha, Sukkot 1:7; above note 1; below 2:1). Whereas the tzitzit coming out of the garment express the 'inner light', that is, the forces that come out into actuality in a defined way that is received within our grasp. 'Tzitzit' is from the term 'the blossom (tzitz) of the field': the grasses that grow and peep out (metzitzim) from the field bring into actuality the forces hidden in it; and so through the mitzvot a person can bring all the forces in him from potential into actuality in a correct and precise way. For example: to reveal in a repaired way the love hidden in a person's heart within marriage, the family and society; to direct the human wish to grow rich in a way that does good; to express national aspirations for the sake of the great vision of repairing the world (following the Maharal, Netiv Ha-Avoda 15).

Therefore the mitzva of tzitzit reminds one of all the mitzvot, as it is said (Bamidbar 15:39): "and you shall see it and remember all the mitzvot of the Lord and do them", and as the Sages expounded (Menaḥot 43b): "Seeing leads to remembering, remembering leads to doing." That is, seeing the tzitzit reminds one of all the mitzvot, whose purpose is to bring the forces in a person into actuality. The Sages further said (there) that seeing the tzitzit reminds one of the reading of the Shema, for the root of the 613 mitzvot is in the mitzva of faith, and the tzitzit arouse a person to express faith in the reading of the Shema, and through this to keep all the mitzvot (following the Maharal, Ḥiddushei Aggadot, Menaḥot 43b).

Like the forces hidden in the material world, faith in God too is hidden and covered, and in consequence man becomes enslaved to the chains of matter in all its conceptions. And Israel, who were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt, were the most enslaved of all, without any ability to express the forces stored up in them. And while they were sunk in enslavement to matter, God revealed Himself to them and brought them out of servitude to redemption, and gave them His Torah and His mitzvot so that they would draw His blessing to all the families of the earth. This is what the Sages said (Sifrei Shelaḥ, piska 115): "Why is it called tzitzit? Because the Omnipresent peeped (hetzitz) at the houses of our fathers in Egypt, as it is said (Shir Ha-Shirim 2:8-9): 'The voice of my beloved, behold, he comes (God who loves us, behold, He comes), leaping over the mountains, skipping over the hills (over all the barriers)… behold, he stands behind our wall, looking in through the windows, peering through the lattices.'"

The idea revealed in the tzitzit is destined to give tidings to all the nations, and this is the meaning of the words of the Sages (Shabbat 32b): "Whoever is careful with tzitzit merits to have two thousand eight hundred servants serve him, as it is said (Zekharya 8:23): 'Thus says the Lord of hosts: In those days ten men from all the languages of the nations shall take hold, and shall take hold of the corner of the garment of a Jewish man, saying: Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.'" At each corner ten men from each of the seventy nations take hold, so at each corner there are seven hundred men, and at the four corners of the garment two thousand eight hundred. And the meaning is not servants in the demeaning sense, but people who understand that without the guidance of the Torah a person becomes enslaved to the chains of this world, without the ability to bring his spiritual forces into actuality. And they understand the virtue of Israel, who are careful with tzitzit and devote themselves to redeeming the forces stored up in man and in the world, and they wish to cleave to them, in order to learn how to bring their talents into actuality and to bring blessing to themselves and to their people (following the Maharal there; Ein Aya, Shabbat 2:221).

sections.title_en: 3. Customs of Dress, and the Mitzva in the 'Tallit Gadol' and the 'Tallit Katan'
sections.body_en:
In the past, the outer garment in which a person covered himself often had four corners, for the complex craft of weaving the garment was done by threads of warp and weft, and so naturally many garments were square. As the craft of tailoring was refined, people chose to give up the corners in order to make garments more fitted to the body and not square. So we have reached a situation in which the garments we are used to wearing today have no four corners and are exempt from tzitzit. In order to merit the mitzva, square garments are made especially: a 'tallit katan' to be worn all day, and a 'tallit gadol' in which to wrap oneself in the Shaḥarit prayer.

Let us explain further: in the period of the Bible and the Mishna they used to wear a ḥaluk, which was a kind of long undershirt, and over it many used to wrap themselves in a tasseled tallit. The ḥaluk served as a basic garment and was exempt from tzitzit, since it did not have four corners. And the tasseled tallit, which had four corners, served as an outer garment meant for protection from cold and sun or for dignity, and when necessary they also wrapped the head in it. And although they often went about in the ḥaluk alone, in honour of prayer they were careful to wrap themselves in a tallit.

It is told in the Talmud (Menaḥot 41a) about Rav Ketina that he used to wear garments exempt from tzitzit. An angel appeared to him and rebuked him: You always wear garments exempt from tzitzit; what will become of the mitzva?! Rav Ketina was astonished: Is a person punished for not fulfilling a mitzva he is not obliged in?! The angel answered him: At a hard time of calamity, even one who appears to be seeking ways to exempt himself from the mitzva is punished. The Rishonim explained that in the time of Rav Ketina it was accepted to go about in garments obliged in tzitzit, and since he chose to evade the mitzva, he aroused an accusation against himself, and at a time of calamity he was liable to be punished for it. But once it was no longer accepted to wear garments with four corners naturally, even at a time of calamity one who did not usually wear such a garment is not punished (see Beit Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayim 24:1).

However, for the Shaḥarit prayer all Israel used to wrap themselves in a tasseled tallit (Shulḥan Arukh 24:1). The Sages said (Zohar III 175a) that one who reads the Shema without tzitzit appears to be bearing false witness about himself, for he reads about the mitzva of tzitzit and does not fulfil it. In addition, many used to wear a 'tallit katan' during the day, until today wearing it has become a clear sign of connection to Jewish identity, to faith and to the mitzvot.2

notes_en.en:
On the customs of dress in the period of the Mishna, see Mishna Me'ila (5:1), Kelim (28:7; 29:1), Teharot (8:13), and the commentators there. And likewise in Tractate Derekh Eretz (7:11). Indeed they did not always wrap themselves in a tallit, but at the time of prayer and in the session of the judges they were careful to wrap themselves in it (Shabbat 10a). And likewise it is told of Rabban Gamliel (Vayikra Rabba 37:3) that before he released a vow he wrapped himself in his tallit. And likewise they said of Mordekhai the Jew (Megilla 16a) and of Nakdimon ben Gurion (Ta'anit 20a) that they wrapped themselves in a tallit before they prayed. Torah scholars were careful that the tallit cover almost all of their ḥaluk (Bava Batra 57b).
In the days of the Rishonim, when they no longer used to wrap themselves in a tallit as clothing, they were careful to wrap themselves in a tallit at the time of the Shaḥarit prayer, and so wrote the Rambam (Tzitzit 3:11; Prayer and the Priestly Blessing 5:5) and the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 24:1; 91:6).
Regarding the 'tallit katan', over the generations there were places where only Torah scholars used to go about in it (as brought in Mayim Ḥayim 2:320, by R. Yosef Messas). But the Ibn Ezra wrote (Bamidbar 15:39) that it is precisely throughout the whole day that it is more important to go about in a tallit katan, through which a person is guarded from sin. Indeed in recent generations many have gone about with a 'tallit katan', and there is one who wrote that this has become a binding custom (Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 4:4).
Regarding the story of Rav Ketina, so many Rishonim explained, among them: Tosafot (Arakhin 2b, s.v. 'Ha-kol'), the Maharam, the Rosh (Mo'ed Katan 3:80), the Semag, the Or Zarua and the Mordekhai. But they added that it is right to go about with a garment of four corners and to become obliged in the mitzva, as Moshe our teacher wanted to enter the Land of Israel so that he could fulfil all the mitzvot (Tosafot Shabbat 32b, s.v. 'Ba'avon'; the Rosh there; Semak; Shulḥan Arukh 24:1; and similarly the Rambam wrote, Tzitzit 3:11). And there are some from whose words it emerges that even in our times, when people are not used to wearing garments obliged in tzitzit, 'at a time of wrath' those who evade the mitzva are liable to be punished (Sha'arei Teshuva of Rabbeinu Yona 3:22; introduction to Sefer Ḥaredim). In any case, it is agreed that just as the mitzva has the power to protect one who volunteers to fulfil it from the temptations of the inclination, so it has the power to protect from calamity.

sections.title_en: 4. Covering the Head with the Tallit, and the Custom of Unmarried Men from Ashkenaz
sections.body_en:
Covering the head with the tallit expresses submission before God; therefore some are meticulous to cover the head with the tallit throughout the prayer, and especially during the Amida prayer (Shulḥan Arukh 8:2; Mishna Berura 8:4).

The custom of unmarried men from communities of Ashkenazi origin is that they fulfil the mitzva of tzitzit with a 'tallit katan' and do not wrap themselves in a 'tallit gadol', for the 'tallit gadol' expresses the 'surrounding light' that a married man merits, who is considered a complete person dwelling in joy and peace (Yevamot 62b; Benei Yissaskhar, Tishrei 13). However, when unmarried men are called up to the Torah or when they serve as shliḥei tzibbur, they wrap themselves in a 'tallit gadol' in honour of the congregation, but they do not cover their heads with it, for this they will merit only after the wedding (Mishna Berura 8:4).3

notes_en.en: A support for the Ashkenazi custom is from the juxtaposition of the verses (Devarim 22:12-13): "You shall make for yourself twisted threads on the four corners of your covering with which you cover yourself. If a man takes a wife" (Tashbetz Katan 462; Minhagei Maharil, Laws of Marriage 10). In order to fulfil the mitzva of tzitzit, unmarried men wear a 'tallit katan' (Eliya Rabba 17:3; Mor U-Ketzi'a 8). Even when an unmarried man needs to wrap himself in a 'tallit gadol', the custom is that he does not cover his head, as is told in the Gemara Kiddushin (29b) about Rav Hamnuna, who did not cover his head because he was not married. However, among the kohanim there are some who are accustomed to wrap themselves in a 'tallit gadol' from when they begin to go up to the dukhan. In recent generations, following the later age of marriage, there were communities in Germany and Hungary in which unmarried men too were accustomed to wrap themselves in a 'tallit gadol' before their wedding, without wrapping the head. And it seems that they did so in order not to postpone for too many years the time of wrapping oneself in a 'tallit gadol' in the Shaḥarit prayer.

sections.title_en: 5. The Blessing over the 'Tallit Gadol' and the 'Tallit Katan'
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of tzitzit is fulfilled with any garment that covers the body, such as a 'tallit katan'. However, since within the dress accepted in the past people used to wrap themselves in large tallitot, in which they at times even wrapped the head and most of the body, the Sages instituted the wording of the blessing 'to wrap ourselves in tzitzit', for this is the way in which the tallit can cover a person the most. Since the blessing says 'to wrap ourselves', the custom after the blessing over a 'tallit gadol' is to be meticulous and wrap oneself in the tallit for the time it takes to walk four amot (two or three seconds). That is, one wraps the head and the upper part of the body in the tallit, in such a way that all the tzitzit are thrown over the left shoulder, and so one stands for the time it takes to walk four amot, and afterwards one again covers oneself with the tallit in the accepted way, with two tzitzit in front and two behind (Shulḥan Arukh 8:4; Mishna Berura 4).4

When putting on a 'tallit katan', the custom is to bless "al mitzvat tzitzit", since one does not usually wrap oneself in it.5

At the time of the blessing it is right to have two intentions in mind: (a) to fulfil the mitzva of tzitzit; (b) to remember through the tzitzit all of God's mitzvot and to grow stronger in doing them, as it is said (Bamidbar 15:39-40): "and you shall see it and remember all the mitzvot of the Lord and do them… so that you remember and do all My mitzvot, and be holy to your God" (Shulḥan Arukh 8:8). Ideally one should say the blessings over mitzvot standing, and this includes the blessing over the 'tallit gadol' and over the 'tallit katan' (Shulḥan Arukh 8:1; Mishna Berura 2).6

notes_en.en: According to the Ra'avya and the Or Zarua (Responsa of the Maharaḥ Or Zarua 4; 8), any garment that is worn not in the manner of wrapping is exempt from tzitzit. Therefore in their view our 'tallit katan' is exempt from tzitzit. And they supported their words from the wording of the blessing: 'to wrap ourselves in tzitzit'. Similar is the view of Geonim brought in the Ittur, that the mitzva of tzitzit is to wrap oneself in the tallit in the manner of the Ishmaelites, that is, with the head wrapped down to the mouth, in the way the Sages spoke (Mo'ed Katan 24a) regarding mourners. But in practice, most of the Rishonim wrote that a 'tallit katan' is obliged in tzitzit, among them: the Ittur, the Maharam, Orḥot Ḥayim, the Nimukei Yosef. This is because the mitzva of tzitzit applies to any covering "with which you cover yourself", "and every garment and covering is implied" (Nimukei Yosef), "sometimes with the head covered, sometimes with the head uncovered" (the Ittur). And the Maharil wrote (New Responsa 4) that one even blesses over it without concern for the view of those who exempt it. And so wrote the Tur and the Shulḥan Arukh (8:2; 6). And so ruled the Aḥaronim. However, out of respect for those who hold that the mitzva is to wrap oneself, and also because the wording of the blessing is 'to wrap ourselves', many Aḥaronim wrote that it is right to wrap oneself in the tallit for the time it takes to walk four amot immediately after the blessing (Gra 8:9). In practice, some fulfil this wrapping by covering the head and face down to the mouth, while throwing all the tzitzit to the left side (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 8:9; Artzot Ha-Ḥayim and Mishna Berura 4). And some are accustomed to cover the head down to the forehead, and when throwing the tallit to the left side they cover the chin and mouth from below (Ish Matzli'aḥ I, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 8:8). And there are further customs, and all are valid.

The Shulḥan Arukh (8:6) wrote that although one does not wrap oneself in a 'tallit katan', one may bless over it 'to wrap ourselves', and in se'if 3 he wrote that it is good to wrap oneself in it for four amot after the blessing. But the Rema (8:6) wrote that the custom is to bless over it 'al mitzvat', for so many Rishonim wrote, among them: the Ritzba (brought in the Kol Bo 22), Rabbeinu Yona (Sefer Ha-Yir'a), the Nimukei Yosef, Ha-Parnes (422), Menorat Ha-Ma'or (Alnaqua, chapter 2). And even according to the Shulḥan Arukh one may bless 'al mitzvat' (Shulḥan Gavoha 8:9; and some disagree). And such is the custom of those of Sephardi origin: when one does not wrap oneself in it, one blesses 'al mitzvat' (Ben Ish Ḥai, Bereshit 6; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 8:25; 27; Alei Hadas 1:21; Yabi'a Omer II, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:1). If one erred and switched the blessings, he has fulfilled his obligation (Ḥayei Adam 12:4; Mishna Berura 8:17).

The Shulḥan Arukh (8:1) wrote that one should wrap oneself and bless standing. But in his source, the Abudarham, he wrote that it is only because of the blessing that one must stand; therefore, if one wraps oneself in a tallit in a way that does not require a blessing, there is no added excellence in standing. And so wrote Halikhot Shlomo (Prayer 3:8, note 14).

sections.body_en:
Those who put on a 'tallit katan' in the morning and shortly afterwards go to pray Shaḥarit and wrap themselves in a 'tallit gadol' should bless over the 'tallit gadol' and intend to exempt the 'tallit katan' as well. But if more than half an hour will pass until they wrap themselves in the 'tallit gadol', it is right that they bless over the 'tallit katan' close to putting it on, and before they begin to pray Shaḥarit they bless over the 'tallit gadol'.

One who removes the 'tallit gadol' for a short time with the intention of wrapping himself in it again, and likewise one whose tallit fell off in the middle of the prayer, should not bless when he wraps himself in it again, for the blessing he said over it at first still serves him, since he did not intend to stop fulfilling the mitzva.

Similarly, one who takes off the 'tallit katan' in the middle of the day in order to put it on again, since his intention is to put it on again, does not bless again. But if he intended to take it off for more than half an hour, for example he intended to swim in a pool, when he puts it on again he blesses. And even if he changed his mind and put it on again after five minutes, since he intended to remove it for more than half an hour, when he puts it on again he blesses. And likewise if he intended to take it off for a short time and in the end was delayed for more than half an hour, when he puts it on again he blesses.7

One who buys or receives a 'tallit gadol' or a 'tallit katan' blesses 'sheheḥeyanu', as one blesses over a new garment (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 22:1).

notes_en.en:
The Shulḥan Arukh wrote (8:14): "If he took off his tallit, even if he had in mind to wrap himself in it again immediately, he must bless when he wraps himself in it again." And such is the view of many Rishonim (Rav Amram Gaon, Shibbolei Ha-Leket, Rabbeinu Yona, Rabbi Avraham Alshvili), and so wrote some Aḥaronim (Yad Aharon, Ḥemed Moshe). Therefore in their view one who removed his tallit in order to go into the toilet must bless when he wraps himself in it again. But in practice this is not the custom (Rema, Baḥ, Mishna Berura 37). Rather, the custom follows one of the following two views: some say that whenever one removed the tallit with the intention of wrapping himself in it again, and the interruption was less than three hours, he does not bless again (Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 8:23; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 52; Halikhot Shlomo 3:7, note 13). And some say that the measure is much shorter, as the Ḥayei Adam wrote (4:6), that "if he did not have in mind to put it on immediately" he must bless, for he is considered to have diverted his attention. And so wrote the Kitzur Shulḥan Arukh (9:10). And so it is implied from the Mishna Berura (8:37) in the name of the Gra. The Aḥaronim of our times estimated this interruption at half an hour (Yabi'a Omer VIII, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:6). And so it seems in practice, for this view is the middle and deciding one between the positions. That is, over every wrapping in tzitzit one must bless, except in a case where he took it off in order to put it on within half an hour. If he took off the tallit without thinking of wrapping himself in it again, even if he stopped for less than half an hour, he blesses over it. But if he took off the tallit during the prayer, presumably his intention was to put it on again, and even without having thought of this explicitly he does not bless over it (Mishna Berura 38).
If the tallit fell off him unintentionally, many hold that he must bless when he wraps himself in it again (Shulḥan Arukh 8:15; Mishna Berura 39). But in practice, in this situation too the custom is not to bless, since he did not want to stop fulfilling the mitzva, and in a doubt about blessings one is lenient (Nimukei Yosef in the name of Rabbeinu Yona, Laws of Tzitzit 12a; Shulḥan Gavoha 8:23; Yafeh La-Lev; Maharsham 4:148; Halikhot Shlomo 3:14; Yabi'a Omer III, Yoreh De'ah 17:11).

sections.title_en: 7. Separating the Threads and Checking Them
sections.body_en:
At times the threads of the tzitzit get tangled with one another, and then one should separate them, because the meaning of the word 'tzitzit' is separate threads, that is, the threads coming out of the gedil should be separate from one another (Tur, Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh 8:7).8

In the past it was common that at times the threads of the tzitzit tore without the wearer noticing, therefore the Rosh wrote: "One who trembles at the word of God should check the tzitzit before wrapping himself, so as not to make a blessing in vain." But today, for the great majority of people it is not common for the threads of the tzitzit to tear unnoticed, and therefore one need not check them every day but only from time to time. And only if something happened that perhaps caused them to tear should he check them immediately. And one whose tzitzit threads commonly tear, or one who does work liable to cause them to tear, should properly check them every day before the blessing.9

notes_en.en: In Menaḥot (42a), Abaye said that one must separate the threads of the tzitzit. The Tur (8:7) explained that the meaning of the word 'tzitzit' is after the separate threads. However, in the view of the Ittur (Laws of Tzitzit 68a), the obligation to separate the tzitzit was at the time they put on tekhelet, and now "it is good to be meticulous and do it as a remembrance of the tekhelet". But in practice it was ruled that even when there is no tekhelet one should separate the tzitzit (New Responsa of the Maharil 6; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 8:7). But the separation is not indispensable to the mitzva, therefore one should not lose prayer with a congregation for it (Magen Avraham 8:10; Eliya Rabba 8; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 12; Mishna Berura 18). When the threads are good, as in our days, they do not tend to tangle, and there is no need to busy oneself with separating them (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 13). However, if in fact they became tangled, for example after laundering, one should separate them.

The Rosh wrote (Laws of Tzitzit 20): "And one who trembles at the word of God should check the tzitzit before wrapping himself, so as not to make a blessing in vain." And in the Responsa of the Rosh (2:9) he wrote that "people were not accustomed to do so… because we keep them in their presumption of validity until it becomes known to him that they have become invalid." So according to the letter of the law one need not check, but it is good to check. The Shulḥan Arukh (8:9) wrote following the Rosh: "Before he blesses, he should look at the threads of the tzitzit to see whether they are valid, so as not to make a blessing in vain." The Taz 8 explained that from the point of view of neglecting the mitzva of tzitzit there is no concern, for one relies on the presumption, but because of the severity of the prohibition of a blessing in vain they were more concerned and required checking. And some say one must check for the fulfilment of the mitzva too (Mishna Berura 22). But all this is a measure of piety, and so wrote Responsa Zera Emet (3:142) and the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (8:14-15). And many great ones were not accustomed to this pious custom (R. Yosef Setehon in 'Va-yelaket Yosef', principle 9; Yeḥaveh Da'at 6:1). And even according to those who hold one must check, since according to the letter of the law one relies on the presumption, one should not lose prayer with a congregation for the checking (Magen Avraham 11). And likewise one called up to the Torah should not check, because of 'the bother to the congregation' (Taz 13:3; Ben Ish Ḥai, Bereshit 3; and see Mishna Berura 8:22). And some say he should check (Mateh Moshe 15; Eliya Rabba 8:10). And it seems that today, when in fact for the great majority of people it is not common for the threads to tear unnoticed, one need not check. As the Magen Avraham wrote (8:11), that one need not check the threads at the place of the hole, for it is not common for the tzitzit to tear there. Even according to the Taz (8:8), who wrote that one must check there, this is only because "it also commonly gets damaged". So everything depends on the question whether it is common for the tzitzit to become invalid, and today for an ordinary person it is not common for the tzitzit to become invalid. But one who does work because of which the tzitzit at times become invalid, and likewise one whose tzitzit threads commonly tear, should properly check them every day.

sections.body_en:
One who stole a tasseled tallit, or stole threads and tied tzitzit with them: the tallit is invalid, as it is said (Bamidbar 15:38): "that they shall make for themselves tzitzit", from which the Sages learned (Sukka 9a): "'for themselves' – from their own". And even one who stole a tallit and put tzitzit of his own on it does not fulfil the mitzva with it, as it is said: "your covering" (Bi'ur Halakha 11:6, s.v. 'Im'). One who buys stolen tzitzit too cannot fulfil the mitzva with them (Mishna Berura 11:30; 25:54). If the seller does not pay taxes, ideally one should not buy from him, for he is like one who steals from the public; but since the tallit itself is not stolen, it is permitted to bless over it.

According to the essential law, one who borrows a garment is exempt from putting tzitzit on it, as it is said (Devarim 22:12): "You shall make for yourself twisted threads on the four corners of your covering", and not on the covering of others. But a garment belonging to partners, such as one belonging to a synagogue, is obliged in tzitzit, as it is said: "on the corners of their garments" (Shulḥan Arukh 14:5; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 10).

One who borrows a tallit from his fellow in order to pray in it or to serve as ḥazan should bless over it, since his fellow gave it to him so that he could fulfil the mitzva with it; presumably he agreed to give it to him in the way that is effective, that is, as 'a gift on condition that it be returned' (the Rosh; Shulḥan Arukh 14:3).

But one who borrows a tallit from his fellow in order to wrap himself in it for the sake of dignity alone, for example for an aliya to the Torah: the poskim disagreed whether he should bless over it. And one who wishes to bless over it should intend to stay in it a few more seconds for the sake of the mitzva, and in this way he will be able to bless according to all views. However, if he has already been called up to the Torah, he should postpone the blessing until after the aliya to the Torah, for if he is delayed in order to bless he will cause 'bother to the congregation'.10

One who needs to wrap himself in a tallit may not take his fellow's tallit without his permission. True, in the past it was accepted that people agreed to this, in order to help their fellows fulfil the mitzva (Shulḥan Arukh 14:4). But in recent generations, with the improvement of hygiene, people have become more sensitive, and many do not agree that their tallit be taken without permission, and therefore a person may not wrap himself in his fellow's tallit without his permission (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 14:11; Ben Ish Ḥai, Lekh Lekha 6).

notes_en.en:
One who borrows a garment is exempt from putting tzitzit on it, but the Sages ruled that after the garment has been borrowed by him for thirty days, since it already looks like his own, he should put tzitzit on it and even bless over it (Ḥullin 136a; Shulḥan Arukh 14:3; Mishna Berura 10). According to Tosafot, the Rosh and others, if he put tzitzit on it before thirty days, ideally he should not bless, and if he blessed he has not lost. And the Agur wrote that the custom is to bless. The Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (14:9) explained that their words were said of the time of the Gemara, when people used to go about with four-cornered garments; but today, when one goes about with such a garment only for the sake of the mitzva, if he borrowed a tallit from his fellow he is obliged immediately to put tzitzit on it and bless over it, for that is why he borrowed it. As the Rosh wrote (Ḥullin 8:26), that if he borrowed a tasseled tallit from his fellow he should bless over it, for the loan is on the understanding that he will fulfil a mitzva with it, and since it must truly be his, he is as though giving it to him as 'a gift on condition that it be returned'. And such is the view of most of the Rishonim, among them: the Roke'aḥ (361) and Rabbeinu Yeruḥam (Toledot Adam Ve-Ḥava 19:3). And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (14:3). And although some hold that he should not bless (Rabbeinu Shimshon; Yam Shel Shlomo, Ḥullin 8:53), in practice most of the Aḥaronim ruled to bless (Mishna Berura 14:11).
Some say that one who borrows a tallit in order to wrap himself in it for the sake of dignity and good manners, for example for an aliya to the Torah, too should bless (Sha'ar Efrayim 19; Eliya Rabba 14:6; Maḥatzit Ha-Shekel 6). And some say he should not bless (Yam Shel Shlomo; Taz 14:4). In order to avoid the dispute, some say it is good to intend not to acquire the tallit, and so he will not need to bless (Derekh Ha-Ḥayim; Mishna Berura 11). And it seems that a ḥazan who wraps himself for the sake of prayer, or a kohen for the sake of the Priestly Blessing, wants to fulfil the mitzva with it, and for this the tallit is given to him, and therefore he should bless (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 10). And for an aliya to the Torah and the like there is indeed a dispute, but if he wishes to stay a few more seconds in the tallit in order to fulfil the mitzva, according to all views he will be able to bless. And if the tallit belongs to the synagogue, even without this he will be able to bless, since it was bought for all who come to the synagogue.

sections.body_en:
The time of the mitzva of tzitzit is by day, as it is said (Bamidbar 15:39): "and you shall see it and remember", that is, at a time when one can naturally see the tzitzit; but a night garment is exempt from tzitzit (Menaḥot 43a). In practice, from the time the day has begun to grow a little light, so that one can distinguish between the threads of tekhelet and the white threads of the tzitzit, the time of the mitzva has come and one may bless over it. This is the time of 'mi-she-yakir' between tekhelet and white. One who puts on a 'tallit katan' or wraps himself in a 'tallit gadol' before then should wait until the time of 'mi-she-yakir' arrives, and then feel the tzitzit and bless (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 18:3. After the fact, if he blessed after 'alot ha-shaḥar' he has fulfilled his obligation, Mishna Berura 10. How the times of 'mi-she-yakir' and 'alot ha-shaḥar' are calculated is explained in Peninei Halakha, Prayer 11:1-2, notes 1-2).

According to the Rambam, the time of wearing is what decides the mitzva. Therefore every square garment worn by day is obliged in tzitzit and one blesses over it, whereas one who wears it at night is exempt from tzitzit and does not bless over it. And according to the Rosh, the garment is what decides, and every garment meant for use by day is obliged in tzitzit even at night, and one blesses over it; whereas a garment meant for the night only, even if it is worn by day, is exempt from tzitzit.

According to halakha, both views are taken into account. Therefore, if according to one view the garment is obliged in tzitzit, one puts tzitzit on it but does not bless over it (Shulḥan Arukh 18:1). For example, one who wears a 'tallit katan' at night, or a ḥazan who wraps himself in a 'tallit gadol' for the Arvit prayer: according to the Rosh, since they are meant to be worn by day, one would bless over wearing them; and according to the Rambam, since one wears them at night they are exempt from tzitzit and one should not bless over them. Therefore in practice they must have valid tzitzit, but one should not bless over them.11

notes_en.en: According to the first Tanna, the mitzva of tzitzit does not depend on time, for its obligation is constant, and so some Amoraim held. But the halakha follows R. Shimon, that the mitzva of tzitzit is only by day, and a 'night garment' is exempt from tzitzit (Menaḥot 43a). According to the Rambam (Tzitzit 3:8), the time of wearing is what decides, and so hold Rav Amram Gaon, the Yere'im, the Ra'avya, the Riaz, Rabbeinu Yona, the Rashba and others. And according to the Rosh (Tzitzit 1), the purpose of the garment is what decides: if it is meant for the day, it is obliged in tzitzit even when one wears it at night, and if it is meant as a 'night garment', it is exempt even when one wears it by day. And so hold Tosafot (Berakhot 14b, s.v. 'Va-yomer'), the Or Zarua, the Semag, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and others. And some Rishonim brought both views without deciding (the Meiri, Hagahot Maimoniyot, the Ritva, the Kol Bo). And according to the Ran and the Teruma, only a day garment by day is obliged in tzitzit. The Shulḥan Arukh (18:1) brought the views of the Rambam and the Rosh in their names without deciding. And the Rema wrote to take both views into account and to bless only over a day garment by day. And the Aḥaronim added that one must put tzitzit on every garment that according to one of the views is obliged in tzitzit (Olat Tamid, Eliya Rabba, Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Ben Ish Ḥai, Mishna Berura 18:2).

sections.title_en: 10. Seeing the Tzitzit: Wearing the Tzitzit Out
sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva that the tzitzit be seen, so that they remind us of all the mitzvot and strengthen us against the temptations of the inclination, as it is said (Bamidbar 15:39): "and you shall see it and remember all the mitzvot of the Lord and do them, and you shall not stray after your heart and after your eyes, after which you go astray." Therefore people are careful that the tzitzit of the 'tallit katan' too be seen. And so it was ruled in the 'Shulḥan Arukh' (8:11): "The essence of the mitzva of the 'tallit katan' is to wear it over one's garments, so that one always sees it and remembers the mitzvot." And so our teacher and rabbi, Rav Tzvi Yehuda Ha-Kohen Kook ztz"l, head of Yeshivat 'Merkaz Ha-Rav', would repeatedly urge his students to take care that the tzitzit be seen. And he would stress that wearing the tzitzit out is not an enhancement of the mitzva but the essence of the mitzva and its completeness, as the Torah itself explained that the purpose of the mitzva is to see the tzitzit and remember the mitzvot.

However, for various reasons there were those who were accustomed to hide the tzitzit of the 'tallit katan'. Some feared the mockery of the gentiles, and some learned from the words of the Ari that according to the Kabbala the 'tallit katan' should be under the garments. Following this, some say that this is the custom of those of Sephardi origin, to keep the tzitzit of the 'tallit katan' concealed (Yaskil Avdi 5:3; Yeḥaveh Da'at 2:1; Shemesh U-Magen II, Oraḥ Ḥayim 74).

But many explained that the words of the Kabbala were said of the garment of the 'tallit katan', which should be under the clothes, but the tzitzit themselves must be brought out so that they are seen, as it is said: "and you shall see it" (Magen Avraham 8:13; Ḥesed La-Alafim 24:3; Artzot Ha-Ḥayim 8:11; Mishna Berura 26).

And it seems that those of Sephardi origin too should take care about this, according to the plain meaning of the verse and as ruled in the 'Shulḥan Arukh', and as some of the poskim of Sephardi origin ruled in practice (as brought in the note). And the fact that they used to conceal the tzitzit is not because they held that this is how one should ideally act, but out of fear of the gentiles, or because they wanted to fulfil the words of the Ari that the 'tallit katan' be under the garment. And since in the lands of the East and North Africa they used to wear a long robe (jellabiya), it was not possible to hide the garment and bring the tzitzit out; rather one had to choose: either to wear the 'tallit katan' over the clothes, as the words of the 'Shulḥan Arukh', or to hide everything and thereby fulfil the words of the Ari. And they acted like the Ari. But had they been accustomed to wear trousers and a shirt, it stands to reason that they would have taken care to bring the tzitzit out.

Besides this, there is great value in wearing the tzitzit out, for it expresses identification with the Torah and reminds one of the mitzvot to do them, as explained in the verse. This is especially important for one who is among people far from Torah and mitzvot: it is good that it be recognisable from his garment that he is meticulous in the mitzvot and is not ashamed to fulfil them, and through this he will be able to overcome his inclination and withstand trials.12

notes_en.en:
Some say that the place of the 'tallit katan' is under the clothes, so that it protects the body from sin and so that it is always on him (the Maharam, the Mordekhai, Rabbeinu Yona, the Radbaz). And some say its place is over the clothes, so that the tzitzit are seen at all times and it is seen by all that he wears the seal of the King (the Ritva, the Nimukei Yosef, R. Yitzḥak ben Meron Ha-Levi). And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (8:11; 24:1). The Levush (8:10) explained that even those who wear it under their clothes must bring out the threads of the tzitzit. And so wrote the Magen Avraham (8:13), Eliya Rabba 12, and others. (The words of my teacher and rabbi, Rav Tzvi Yehuda, are brought in Teḥumin 3; Mi-Tokh Ha-Torah Ha-Go'elet II, Vayishlaḥ.)
In practice, for three reasons many were accustomed to wear the 'tallit katan' under their clothes and to hide its tzitzit: (a) because they feared the gentiles, who mocked it (Meshivat Nefesh of Rabbi Yoḥanan Luria, Shemot 2:19; Shulḥan Gavoha 8:17; Derashot Ḥatam Sofer I, p. 187; Mayim Ḥayim of R. Yosef Messas 2:320). (b) Some understood from the words of the Ari that according to the Kabbala one must conceal the tallit and the tzitzit under the clothes (Ma'amar Mordekhai 24:1). (c) In the previous generation there were those who wrote that this is the custom of those of Sephardi origin, to conceal the tzitzit (Yaskil Avdi 5:3; Shemesh U-Magen II, Oraḥ Ḥayim 74; Yeḥaveh Da'at 2:1; Mikveh Ha-Mayim 3:1).
But in practice, when we consider the three reasons according to which they concealed the tzitzit, we conclude that it is right to rule today for members of all communities to bring out the threads of the tzitzit so that they are seen. (a) Those who were accustomed to conceal the tzitzit because of the mockery of the gentiles held that in principle one must bring the tzitzit out; if so, when there is no reason to fear this, it is a mitzva that the tzitzit be seen. (b) The Ari stressed in Sha'ar Ha-Kavanot (Tzitzit 7): "One must look at the tzitzit at every hour and moment, as it is written, 'and you shall see it'", which implies that in his view one must bring the tzitzit out. And so wrote Or Tzaddikim following him (Tzitzit 7:9-17). And so wrote Artzot Ha-Ḥayim (8:11) and Pekudat Elazar (8:11).
(c) Even regarding the custom of those of Sephardi origin, we find many of the great ones of Sephardi origin who ruled to bring the tzitzit out, and explained that this is right according to the Kabbala too. So wrote Rav Papo in Ḥesed La-Alafim (24:3), and so it emerges from the Ḥida, as Aseh Lekha Rav (3:2) explained. And so wrote Pekudat Elazar (8:11) from Morocco, Rav Moshe Khalfon of Djerba (Berit Kehuna 9:4), Nefesh Ḥaya (9:6) from Tunis and Netivot, Yitzḥak Yeranen (siman 2) from Aleppo. And so the rabbis of Yemen wrote in practice: Piskei Maharitz (Tzitzit 14), Shetilei Zeitim (8:11). Moreover, it seems that the rabbis of Sephardi origin did not choose to conceal the tzitzit; rather, since they used to wear a long robe (jellabiya), they had two options: to wear the 'tallit katan' with its tzitzit under the robe or over it, and they chose to wear it underneath, as the words of the Ari. But had they been able to bring the tzitzit out, in the way of those accustomed to wear a shirt and trousers, they would have done so. And so wrote Az Nidberu (7:90; 8:39). Similarly the Shela wrote that he used to lengthen greatly the two front tzitzit so that they would be seen below the robe (Siddur Sha'ar Ha-Shamayim, the intention of prayer).
In addition, even among those who hold that those of Sephardi origin were not accustomed to bring the tzitzit out, they did not see this as a binding custom; and therefore when they held that bringing the tzitzit out could strengthen religious identity, they instructed to bring them out, as Aseh Lekha Rav (3:2) and Or Le-Tziyon (II 2:2) wrote. However, one whose father or teacher insists that he tuck in the tzitzit should, out of respect for them, act as they do.

sections.title_en: 11. A Tallit Whose Tzitzit Have Become Invalid
sections.body_en:
The four tzitzit that it is a mitzva to put on the four corners of the garment are each indispensable to the others, for the four of them are one mitzva (Menaḥot 28a). Therefore, if one of the tzitzit became invalid (see below 2:12), it is forbidden to wear the garment, and if one transgressed and wore it, he has neglected a positive mitzva. And if he went out with it on Shabbat into the public domain in a place where there is no eruv, he has also transgressed the prohibition of 'carrying', because of the tzitzit remaining on the garment. For as long as the tzitzit are valid they are part of the garment and it is permitted to go out with them on Shabbat into the public domain; but if they became invalid they become superfluous and it is forbidden to carry them (Shabbat 139b; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 13:1-2).

One who was wearing a tallit and saw that one of the tzitzit had torn off the corner of his garment, or that its threads had torn so that it became invalid, must remove it immediately, because every moment he leaves it on him he is neglecting a positive mitzva (Menaḥot 37b). And if this causes him great embarrassment, for example he is speaking before an audience, he may wait until he can remove it (and if he discovered on Shabbat that the tzitzit is invalid, see the note).13

It is permitted to untie tzitzit from one tallit in order to tie them on another tallit, but without a reason it is forbidden to remove them, for one should not treat the tzitzit with contempt for nothing (Menaḥot 41b; Shulḥan Arukh 15:1). If the threads of the tzitzit wore out and lost their beauty, it is permitted to cut them in order to tie beautiful threads in their place (Mishna Berura 15:3; see Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 13:11).

Threads of tzitzit that were cut, and likewise an invalid tallit that wore out, do not need geniza, since they are 'objects used for a mitzva' and not 'objects of holiness' (below 14:8). Therefore one may put them in the bin in a respectful way, and if there were filthy things in the bin, he should wrap them in paper or a bag and put them in the bin like that. Likewise, one should not use them for degrading things, such as making the tallit into a floor rag (see Shulḥan Arukh and Rema 21:1-3).14

notes_en.en: When a mitzva or a prohibition clashes with human dignity, there are three levels in the matter: (a) a 'negative commandment' from the Torah: it is forbidden to transgress even in a place of great embarrassment. (b) A positive commandment from the Torah: it is permitted to neglect it in order to prevent great embarrassment. (c) A rabbinic prohibition: it is permitted to transgress even in order to prevent ordinary embarrassment. Therefore, one walking in the public domain on Shabbat who saw that the tzitzit had become invalid: since if he continues walking he will transgress the Torah 'negative commandment' of carrying in the public domain, even when this involves great embarrassment he must remove the tallit immediately. And if it is a public domain by rabbinic law (a 'karmelit'), in a place where there is embarrassment in removing the tzitzit, even when it is not great embarrassment, he may continue walking in it to his home and remove it there, for great is human dignity, which overrides a rabbinic prohibition (Menaḥot 37b; Shulḥan Arukh 13:3). And this is not considered neglect of a 'positive commandment', because the positive commandment from the Torah is to put tzitzit on the garment, and since on Shabbat it is forbidden to tie tzitzit, he is not considered to be neglecting a Torah positive commandment; only in carrying does he transgress a rabbinic prohibition (Mordekhai in the name of the Ri; Beit Yosef 13:3; Mishna Berura 9). And today, according to most of the poskim, our streets are considered a 'karmelit' (Peninei Halakha, Shabbat 21:9). And likewise one who saw on Shabbat that his tallit had become invalid, and is embarrassed to sit in the synagogue without a tallit, and has no possibility of receiving a borrowed tallit, may wrap himself in the invalid one without a blessing (Rema 13:3). And if he saw on a weekday that the tzitzit is invalid, when it is possible to tie tzitzit, at every single moment that he does not remove it he is neglecting a Torah positive commandment, and then only in a case of great embarrassment is he permitted to stay in it; but if the embarrassment is ordinary, he must remove it (Magen Avraham 8; Mishna Berura 15).

The Shulḥan Arukh wrote (21:1), following Megilla (26b), that the threads of the tzitzit do not need geniza and it is permitted to throw them into the rubbish. Whereas the Orḥot Ḥayim (I, Tzitzit 34) wrote that one should not treat them disrespectfully. The Rema wrote that accordingly it is forbidden to throw them into a disgusting place, and according to the Maharil it is right to be meticulous and put them in geniza. But one can say that they do not disagree, and it is permitted to throw them into rubbish in which there are no filthy things, but not into rubbish in which there is filth. And since in the past there was often filth in the rubbish, some ruled to put them in geniza. Therefore what I wrote above is agreed by most of the poskim. And see Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 13:11.

sections.body_en:
It is right to beautify the mitzva and to fulfil it with a beautiful tallit and beautiful tzitzit (Mishna Berura 24:9), as it is said (Shemot 15:2): "This is my God and I will glorify Him, the God of my father and I will exalt Him." The Sages expounded (Shabbat 133b): "Adorn yourself before Him in mitzvot: make before Him a beautiful sukka, a beautiful lulav, a beautiful shofar, beautiful tzitzit, a beautiful Sefer Torah." Included in this, one should take care that the tallit not be worn out or stained or blackened by sweat (Seder Ha-Yom). Rather, his tallit should be beautiful and clean. And how much disgrace and shame there is for one who is used to buying expensive clothes and takes care that they be clean and beautiful, and does not take care that his tallit be beautiful and clean (Ḥesed La-Alafim 24:5).

Out of love for the mitzva, the custom is to hold the tzitzit during the reading of the Shema and to kiss them when mentioning the tzitzit and their subject. Indeed in the days of the Geonim there were those who opposed this and argued that one should not invent customs that have no root in the Talmud, and that one who practises them sins with arrogance (Rav Natronai Gaon). But since many in Israel already practised them, the customs became accepted and there is no arrogance in them (Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh 24:2-4; see Peninei Halakha, Prayer 15:11).

In order to understand the degree of care for the honour of the tzitzit, one must first note that anything containing holy names, such as a Sefer Torah, tefillin or a mezuza, is called an 'object of holiness', and one must take great care to honour it. Therefore it is forbidden to enter the toilet with tefillin or a siddur. But other things with which mitzvot are performed, such as tzitzit and sekhakh, are called 'objects used for a mitzva', and one need not be so careful about their honour (below 14:8). Therefore it is permitted to sit in such a way that the tzitzit are lying on the ground, and likewise it is permitted to sleep with a 'tallit katan' or to enter the toilet with it. However, it is forbidden to treat the tzitzit with contempt, for example to tie something with its threads. Likewise one should not walk in such a way that the tzitzit drag on the ground (She'iltot; Shulḥan Arukh 21:1; 4). The custom is not to enter the toilet with a 'tallit gadol', but not because of the holiness of the tzitzit, rather because of the honour of the tallit, which is set aside for prayer (Taz 3; Mishna Berura 14). It is fitting not to sneeze into the tallit or to wipe one's face with it, but there is no prohibition in this, since the tallit is a garment, and this is what people do with a garment.

One who enters a cemetery or comes within four amot of a dead person must hide his tzitzit inside his garment, and likewise he should not put on tefillin there, nor study Torah, nor fulfil other mitzvot (Shulḥan Arukh 23:1; 45:1; 71:7). For since the dead person cannot fulfil mitzvot, one who fulfils mitzvot beside him appears to be 'mocking the poor' (Berakhot 18a).

sections.title_en: 13. Women Are Exempt from the Mitzva of Tzitzit
sections.body_en:
Women are exempt from the mitzva of tzitzit, since women are exempt from positive mitzvot that are 'caused by time', and the obligation of tzitzit depends on time, for it applies by day and not at night (Menaḥot 43a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 17:2; Peninei Halakha, Women's Prayer 2:7).

Women who wish to wrap themselves in a tallit may do so. According to the custom of women of Ashkenazi origin they bless over the tzitzit, and according to the custom of women of Sephardi origin they do not bless (Peninei Halakha, Women's Prayer 2:8). However, it is accepted that women do not fulfil the mitzva of tzitzit in public, because of arrogance. That is, since nearly all righteous women are not accustomed to wrap themselves in tzitzit, one who wraps herself in tzitzit in public appears to be showing off.15

notes_en.en:
According to the first Tanna, the mitzva of tzitzit does not depend on time, for its obligation is constant. And so held Rav Amram Ḥasida, who put tzitzit on the garments of the women of his household (Menaḥot 43a; Sukka 11a). And according to R. Shimon, the time of the mitzva of tzitzit is by day, and therefore women are exempt from it (Menaḥot there). And so is the halakha (Shulḥan Arukh 17:1; above halakha 9). However, like all positive mitzvot caused by time, women who wish may fulfil it as an optional mitzva, and the only dispute is whether they may bless. True, the Maharil wrote in his Responsa (New Responsa 7) that women should not wrap themselves in a tallit, because there is reason to be concerned about the prohibition of kilayim and carrying on Shabbat, and about the custom of simple people and arrogance, and a further reason according to the Kabbala. And in Sefer Maharil (Minhagim, Laws of Tzitzit 4) it is told that there were women who wrapped themselves in tzitzit, among them Rabbanit Bruna, and although he was not pleased with her custom, he did not protest, lest she not listen. And see further the Agur (Laws of Tzitzit 27), who mentioned a custom of women who wrapped themselves in tzitzit, and wrote that one should not do so because of arrogance, and so wrote the Rema (17:1). So there is no concern of prohibition in this; only because it appears to be arrogance did they rule that they should not wrap themselves in tzitzit. And so many Aḥaronim wrote. The Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (17:2-3) explained that mitzvot that men are obliged to fulfil, such as hearing the shofar and taking the lulav, women were accustomed to fulfil, and mitzvot that are not an obligation for men, such as tzitzit, they were not accustomed to fulfil. Thus far. However, there are testimonies about righteous women who would wrap themselves in tzitzit (R. Yosef Messas, Naḥalat Avot V, p. 268). In Igrot Moshe (Oraḥ Ḥayim 4:49) he wrote that if the woman's aim in wrapping herself in tzitzit is for the sake of Heaven, she may do so and has a reward for it; but if she does so out of an outside influence, in order to fight the battle of feminism and to undermine the words of the Torah and claim that women too are obliged like men, she has no mitzva in her hand but a forbidden act of denial of the Torah. Thus far.
In practice, one should not criticise those who fulfil the mitzva modestly, and even if they do so out of identification with the positive sides of the feminist movement, one should not mix the struggle against the negative sides of the feminist movement into the discussion of fulfilling the mitzva of tzitzit. See the words of our master Rav Kook ('Yissurim Memarkim', Zer'onim, Orot), that one should not reject any movement that seeks to add good, for in all of them there are Divine sparks, and in rejecting them there is a flaw in faith that causes crises and suffering; rather, the repair is to shed upon them abundant light from the source of Israel, so that they indeed add goodness and blessing. And if many women act this way modestly for the sake of Heaven, in the course of time, even if they act this way in public, it will no longer be considered arrogance. It further seems that one should not protest against a woman who wraps herself in a tallit in public, because the concern of arrogance does not justify a protest. Even when it concerns women who make light of various mitzvot and wrap themselves in a tallit in public demonstratively, although making light of the mitzvot deserves criticism in a way that is effective, one should not protest against their wrapping themselves in tzitzit, since wrapping oneself in tzitzit in itself is not a transgression but a mitzva. (On the reasons for the few differences between the mitzvot of men and women, see Peninei Halakha, Women's Prayer chapter 3; Simḥat Ha-Bayit U-virkhato chapter 10.)
In the Targum Yonatan ben Uziel (Devarim 22:5) it is implied that there is a prohibition for women to wrap themselves in a tallit because of 'a man's garment shall not be worn'. But all the Rishonim who dealt with the issue did not mention this concern. Among the Aḥaronim, however, there were those who mentioned it, among them the Ben Ish Ḥai (Lekh Lekha 13), and according to their view it is right that women who wear a tallit combine further colours in it, in order to distinguish between a men's tallit and a women's. But nearly all the poskim did not mention this problem, and the Maharam Schick explained (Yoreh De'ah 173), following the Taz (182:4), that the prohibition of 'shall not be worn' is when one wears a garment for the sake of adornment, and not when one wears it for the sake of a mitzva.
